title: Algebraic Expressions and Polynomials — Chapter Summary
intro: Algebra extends arithmetic by letting letters stand for numbers. Built from variables and constants with +, −, ×, ÷ and powers, algebraic expressions let us state rules once and apply them to every case. This chapter develops the vocabulary, classifies expressions, defines the special class called polynomials and shows how to add, subtract, multiply and evaluate them.

branches.label: Evaluation & zeros
details: Value of p at x = a is p(a)
A zero is x with p(x) = 0

sections.heading: Algebraic Expressions — Vocabulary
bullets: A variable (x, y, a, n…) stands for a number; a constant is a fixed number such as 3, −7 or √2.
An algebraic expression is built from constants and variables using +, −, ×, ÷ and powers.
A term is a part of the expression separated by + or −; the sign immediately before a term belongs to it.
Each term is a product of a coefficient (numerical part) and a variable part with non-negative integer powers.
Like terms have the same variable part; they combine by adding or subtracting their coefficients.
A constant term has no variable part — it is just a number, e.g. the −9 in 5p^3 − 2p^2 + p − 9.

sections.heading: Classifying Expressions by Number of Terms
bullets: Monomial — exactly one term (e.g. 5x, −7p^3, 2/3).
Binomial — two unlike terms (e.g. 3x + 5, p^2 − 7p).
Trinomial — three unlike terms (e.g. x^2 + 3x − 2).
Multinomial — more than three unlike terms.
Always combine like terms first before counting; 2x + 3x + 5 is a binomial (5x + 5), not a trinomial.

sections.heading: Polynomials and Degree
bullets: A polynomial uses only non-negative integer powers of its variables and never divides by a variable.
Non-examples: 3/x, √x, x^(−2) + 5, 2/(x + 1) — each fails one of the two rules above.
Degree (one variable): the largest exponent that appears, e.g. degree of 5z^4 + z^2 − 1 is 4.
Degree (several variables): the largest sum-of-exponents across the terms; degree of 4xy + 7x^2 y^3 is 5.
Special names by degree: 0 = constant, 1 = linear, 2 = quadratic, 3 = cubic, 4 = biquadratic.
Standard form: terms written in descending order of degree, making leading coefficient and constant term easy to read off.

sections.heading: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials
bullets: Adding / subtracting polynomials means combining their like terms.
Horizontal method: write the polynomials side by side, group like terms, simplify.
Vertical method: stack so like terms align in columns and add column by column — handy for long polynomials.
To subtract, change the sign of every term being subtracted, then add.
The sum or difference of polynomials is again a polynomial, with degree at most the larger of the two.

sections.heading: Multiplying Polynomials
bullets: Use the distributive law: every term of the first polynomial multiplies every term of the second.
Monomial × polynomial: distribute the monomial across each term — 3x^2(2x + 5) = 6x^3 + 15x^2.
Binomial × binomial: FOIL (First, Outer, Inner, Last). For (x + 2)(x + 3): x^2 + 3x + 2x + 6 = x^2 + 5x + 6.
Long polynomials × long polynomials: use the vertical long-multiplication layout.
Exponent rules x^a · x^b = x^(a+b) and (xy)^n = x^n y^n drive every multiplication: (3x^2 y)(5xy^4) = 15 x^3 y^5.
Degree(product) = Degree(p) + Degree(q).

sections.heading: Evaluating Polynomials and Zeros
bullets: To evaluate p(x) at x = a, substitute a for x and simplify the arithmetic — p(a) is a single number.
A zero (root) of p(x) is any value of x for which p(x) = 0.
Example: for p(x) = x^2 − 4x + 4, p(2) = 4 − 8 + 4 = 0, so x = 2 is a zero (a repeated zero in this case).
A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeros (counting multiplicities).

key_takeaways: Algebraic expressions are arithmetic-with-letters: variables stand for numbers and constants are fixed numbers.
A polynomial uses only non-negative integer powers and never divides by a variable.
Degree is the largest exponent (one variable) or the largest sum-of-exponents across terms (several variables).
Add or subtract polynomials by combining like terms; subtraction flips signs first.
Multiply polynomials by distributing every term of one across every term of the other; the laws of exponents handle the variable parts.
Evaluating a polynomial at a number is just arithmetic; an x for which p(x) = 0 is called a zero.

glossary.definition: A symbol (typically a letter) that stands for a number.
A fixed number such as 3, −7, 2/5 or √2.
An expression built from constants and variables using +, −, ×, ÷ and powers.
A part of an algebraic expression that is separated from other parts by + or − signs.
The numerical (constant) part of a term, including its sign.
A term with no variable part; just a number.
Terms that have the same variable part and so can be combined by adding or subtracting their coefficients.
An algebraic expression with exactly one term, e.g. 5x or −7p^3.
An algebraic expression with exactly two unlike terms, e.g. 3x + 5.
An algebraic expression with exactly three unlike terms, e.g. x^2 + 3x − 2.
An algebraic expression in which each variable appears only with non-negative integer powers and no variable lies in a denominator.
The largest exponent (one variable) or the largest sum-of-exponents over all terms (several variables) in a polynomial.
A polynomial in one variable written with its terms in descending order of degree.
The coefficient of the highest-degree term of a polynomial in standard form.
A value of the variable for which the polynomial evaluates to 0.
